John Cennick
JON SEN-ik
proper noun
John, Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious”; Cennick, a surname of Bohemian or Quaker-English derivation.

Biblical Definition

John Cennick (1718–1755) was an English evangelist and hymn-writer of the early revival, who labored first among the Methodists alongside the Wesleys and Whitefield, then moved into the orbit of the Moravian Brethren, preaching the gospel widely in England and Ireland in the face of much opposition and mob violence. Converted out of inward distress, he became a tireless itinerant who counted it joy to suffer for Christ, and his hymns carry the fervor of one who had tasted the pardoning grace of God. He gave the church “Children of the Heavenly King,” a marching song of the redeemed who follow their Captain on the pilgrim road toward the city of God, singing as they travel and bidding one another lift their hearts. Cennick also penned the first draft of “Lo! He Comes with Clouds Descending,” the great hymn of the Lord’s return in glory, later revised into its familiar form; it summons the saints to hail the descending King and looks for the day when every eye shall see Him. Cennick’s associations with Moravian piety carried with them a stress on the wounds and blood of Christ that at times tended toward excess, an error the sound church will mark; yet his enduring hymns set forth solid gospel truth, the pilgrim character of the Christian life and the certain coming of the King. He died at thirty-six, worn out in the work of an evangelist.

Webster 1828 Definition

An early Methodist and Moravian evangelist and hymn-writer (1718–1755), author of “Children of the Heavenly King” and the first draft of “Lo! He Comes with Clouds Descending.”

JOHN CENNICK, an English evangelist and hymn-writer (1718–1755) of the early revival.

Labored with the Methodists and then among the Moravian Brethren, preaching in England and Ireland.

Wrote “Children of the Heavenly King,” a pilgrim hymn of the redeemed on the road to glory.

Penned the first draft of “Lo! He Comes with Clouds Descending,” the hymn of Christ’s return.

Endured mob violence as an itinerant and died worn out at thirty-six.

Key Scripture

Rev 1:7 — "Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him, and they also which pierced him: and all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of him. Even so, Amen."

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

1Pe 2:11 — "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul."

Mat 25:13 — "Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh."

Modern Corruption

The truth to recover is the pilgrim character of the Christian life and the sure return of Christ in glory — an expectancy the church easily loses.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is that believers are children of a heavenly King, strangers and pilgrims marching toward a city not their own. Cennick’s hymn refuses the settled worldliness that forgets the journey’s end and bids the saints sing as they travel home.

His second great hymn fixes the eye on the coming King. “Lo! He Comes with Clouds Descending” takes up the plain words of Revelation, that every eye shall see Him. A church that has muted the doctrine of Christ’s return loses both its warning and its hope; Cennick recalls it to watchfulness and to the cry, “Even so, Amen.”

Hebrew Roots

The hymns’ governing themes are the pilgrim road and the descending King, drawn from Hebrews and Revelation.

expand to see more

John Cennick — the surname likely of Bohemian or Czech derivation.

“Strangers and pilgrims” renders the Greek parepidemoi of Hebrews 11:13 and 1 Peter 2:11.

“He cometh with clouds” quotes Revelation 1:7 directly.

“Children of the Heavenly King” echoes the adoption of the redeemed as sons.

His draft of “Lo! He Comes” was later reworked by Charles Wesley and Martin Madan.

Usage

"John Cennick sang of the redeemed as children of the Heavenly King on their pilgrim way."

"The hymn of Christ’s glorious return owes its first form to John Cennick."

"John Cennick endured mobs and stoning to carry the gospel through England and Ireland."
